name: Buddha Head Fig, Wat Mahathat

location.address: Wat Mahathat, Chikun Road, Ayutthaya Historical Park, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya

verified_sources: https://th.wikipedia.org/wiki/รุกข_มรดกของแผ่นดิน (reproduces the 2017 register table of the Department of Cultural Promotion, Ministry of Culture; source file data.go.th tree1.xlsx, 403 to curl)

official_register.name: Rukkha Moradok khong Phaendin (Heritage Trees of the Land), Department of Cultural Promotion, Ministry of Culture, 2017 list, Ayutthaya entry 'Pho'

access: Paid entry to the Fine Arts Department's Ayutthaya Historical Park ticket (foreign adult price reported by 2026 guides as about 80 THB, Thai nationals about 10 THB; confirm at the gate); open daily roughly 08:00 to 18:00-18:30 (hours differ between guides, no official page found); modest dress (shoulders and knees covered); viewing platform is a low rope-line, do not stand higher than the head.
transport: Ayutthaya railway station then the 5-minute river ferry and about 2 km by tuk-tuk, bicycle or walking; Bangkok to Ayutthaya by train about 1.5 hours. Temple stands opposite Wat Ratchaburana on Chikun Road.
verify_notes: Famous sandstone Buddha head held in the roots of a fig at Wat Mahathat. Register (2017, Ministry of Culture list, province Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya) records the tree as 'Pho' (bodhi, Ficus religiosa) with girth 9.60 m (a buttressed root mass around the head, not a single trunk), height 15 m, age 'not stated' (ไม่ระบุ), coordinates 14.356670,100.568247. SPECIES CONFLICT: the register and the on-site sign call it a bodhi; travel writers (Under the Banyan, Your Thai Guide) call it a banyan or strangler fig; iNaturalist identifications on the spot are split between Ficus benghalensis, Ficus rumphii and plain Ficus (none research grade), so species given as Ficus sp. and the page asks the reader. Pin: register point is about 10 m from a cluster of iNaturalist GPS fixes (3 to 5 m accuracy, 2025-02 to 2026-07) at 14.3567,100.5682, so confirmed. Alive: iNat observations 2026-03-19 and 2026-07-23; a search summary (Matichon, 2024, unfetched, Cloudflare) reports Forest Department help for a storm-damaged tree at the head in 2024, to be treated as a pointer only. AGE: none documented anywhere; one guide says the tree grew around the head over about 250 years but cites no source (not used). The head itself is dated variously from the 14th to 17th century; the popular account ties it to the 1767 sack of Ayutthaya (head fallen, roots grew round it); a Pattaya guide says a worker set the head in the roots around 1968 to 1970, which conflicts. One Thai news item calls the natural tree 'over 50 years' old (Thairath, unfetched). Do not state an age or the 1767 link as fact. Register only plus iNat sightings, so flagged. Wat Mahathat is part of the UNESCO World Heritage city (1991).
story:
Nobody agrees how a sandstone Buddha's head came to sit in the roots of this tree. The story most visitors hear is that the head fell when the Burmese army sacked Ayutthaya in 1767, and that the tree slowly grew around it. It is a popular account, not a recorded one. One guide says instead that a worker set the head among the roots around 1968 to 1970. The head itself is dated anywhere from the 14th to the 17th century.

The tree is just as unsettled. Thailand's Ministry of Culture lists it among its Heritage Trees of the Land as a bodhi, and so does the sign on site. Travel writers call it a banyan or a strangler fig, and naturalists who have photographed it disagree three ways. Which fig it is, nobody has settled, and nobody has dated it either. If you know, tell us.

What is measured is the root mass. The register gives 9.60 metres round, a buttressed tangle wrapped about the face rather than one trunk, on a tree 15 metres tall.

It stands in the ruins of Wat Mahathat, opposite Wat Ratchaburana on Chikun Road, inside the Ayutthaya Historical Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1991. The park ticket was about 80 baht for foreign adults in 2026, and hours run roughly 08:00 to 18:00, so check at the gate. The custom is to keep your own head lower than the Buddha's, photograph included.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the stone Buddha's face held in the roots, behind a low rope line. It stands in the ruins of Wat Mahathat, opposite Wat Ratchaburana on Chikun Road.

location_site.name: Wat Phra Ngam ruined temple precinct

verify_notes: A bodhi that has grown over and around a brick gateway (a lotus-petal-arched gate) of the abandoned Wat Phra Ngam, nicknamed 'the gate of time' by Thai travel press. Listed in the 2019 Heritage Trees of the Land (88 trees); the national table in th.wikipedia gives only the name for 2019 (no coordinates, girth or age). Register has no figures. Age: travel articles say 'at least 100 years' with no scientific basis, so age_min 100 only, not a derived age. The temple is thought abandoned at the 1767 fall of Ayutthaya (unsourced popular account); do not link tree to 1767. Pin is the OSM centroid of the archaeological site (way 744402568), not the gate; precision approximate with a small named site, recognise by the bodhi trunks embracing the arched brick gateway. ALIVE NOT CONFIRMED by a dated tree observation (lifecheck NONE; one iNat Ficus rumphii 2023-01-09 about 80 m away is not proof); only register 2019 and undated travel pages. Register only, so flagged. Recheck with a dated photo or news item before write-up.
story:
This bodhi tree has swallowed a doorway. Its roots and trunks have grown over and around a brick gateway of the ruined Wat Phra Ngam, so that the trunks now frame its arch, shaped like a lotus petal. Thai travel writers call it the gate of time.

In 2019 Thailand's Ministry of Culture added it to its list of Heritage Trees of the Land, one of 88 trees named that year. The list gives no measurements and no age. Travel articles put the tree at 100 years or more, but nobody has measured or dated it, so treat that as a guess.

The temple itself is a ruin, and a popular account says it was abandoned after Ayutthaya fell to the Burmese in 1767. That is an account, not a record, and nothing connects this tree to that date. What you see is simpler, a sacred fig, the species the Buddha is said to have sat under, wrapped around a brick doorway.

Wat Phra Ngam lies in Khlong Sa Bua, on the north bank across from the old city island, about 2 kilometres north of Wat Mahathat. Travel guides report no ticket, and the compound sits beside the road. Go by day, dress as you would for any temple, and take a tuk-tuk or bicycle from the island, about ten minutes. If you go, tell us how the tree looks.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bodhi trunks wrapped over and around an arched brick gateway. It stands at the gate of the ruined Wat Phra Ngam in Khlong Sa Bua.
